18.0.0.en: Now after this it came to pass, that David smote the Philistines, and subdued them, and took Gath and her towns out of the hand of the Philistines. [1]

18.0.1.en: David enjoyed continual victories ever since he began, as a young man, his battle with Goliath the Philistine giant, for the Lord helps him wherever he goes.

18.0.2.en: Many of the Fathers see that David’s warring against the pagan nations and his victory over them signify the work of the Lord Christ as the leader of the spiritual battle against the devil and his angels, to free us from our slavery to him and to sin.

18.0.3.en: v Christ, the true David, came to lift the human race out of the valley of sins and tears. He stood in a valley facing the Philistines (1 Sam 17:19-20). They were in a valley, because the weight of their sins pressed them down. At any rate, (the Israelites) were standing, but they did not dare to fight their adversaries.

18.0.4.en: Why did they not dare to do this? Because David, the type of Christ, had not yet arrived.

18.1.0.en: This is true, beloved brethren. Who was able to fight against the devil before Christ our Lord freed the human race from his authority? Now the word David is translated “strong of hand,” and who is stronger, brethren, than the One who overcame the whole world, armed with the Cross and not with a sword?[2]

18.1.1.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles. His victory over the Philistines [1]. It was already discussed in (1 Chr 14:9-16).

18.1.2.en: His victory over the Moabites [2]. This is depicted in a lesser manner than it was recorded in (1 Sam 22:3).

18.2.0.en: He moved toward the north, and overcame the people of Zobah [3] and the Syrians [5].

18.2.1.en: All these nations submitted to his authority, so David reigned as far as the river Euphrates.

18.3.0.en: And he smote Moab; and the Moabites became David’s servants, and brought gifts. [2]

18.3.1.en: The Second Book of Samuel (2 Sam 8:1-2) recorded for us that David killed two thirds of the Moabites, though his grandmother Ruth was a Moabitess.

18.4.0.en: v It is fitting for us to recognize that those wars are a symbolic description of the victories of the Lord the Savior, since He overcame idolatry and unbelief in the whole world. These are their words that He speaks (Psalm 60), for in truth He removed their old superstitions so that they might be made fit for the change through the grace of the new man[3].

18.5.0.en: Father Cassiodorus v In the Second Book of Kings (Second Samuel), where David defeated the Moabites, the Holy Bible records for us the measuring of two separate lines, one for life and the other for death (2 Sam 8:2) LXX. The meaning of leaving some of the Moabites alive while the others died is made clear through the story of Orpah and Ruth. Orpah, who returned again to idolatry and to her old city, was appointed to death. But Ruth, who followed her mother-in-law, and whose name means “Naomi (joyful),” says: “Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God” (Ruth 1:16)[4].

18.6.0.en: 3 And David smote Hadarezer king of Zobah unto Hamath, as he went to stablish his dominion by the river Euphrates. 4 And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: David also houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them an hundred chariots. 5 And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadarezer king of Zobah, David slew of the Syrians two and twenty thousand men. 6 Then David put garrisons in Syriadamascus; and the Syrians became David’s servants, and brought gifts. Thus the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went. 7 And David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadarezer, and brought them to Jerusalem. 8 Likewise from Tibhath, and from Chun, cities of Hadarezer, brought David very much brass, wherewith Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass. 9 Now when Tou king of Hamath heard how David had smitten all the host of Hadarezer king of Zobah; 10 He sent Hadoram his son to king David, to enquire of his welfare, and to congratulate him, because he had fought against Hadarezer, and smitten him; (for Hadarezer had war with Tou;) and with him all manner of vessels of gold and silver and brass.

18.6.1.en: And David smote Hadarezer king of Zobah unto Hamath, as he went to stablish his dominion by the river Euphrates. [3]

18.6.2.en: Hadarezer: this name is derived from the word “Hadad,” which is the name of a Syrian god, and at one time it became the special title of the rulers of this kingdom, like “Pharaoh” for the kings of Egypt.

18.6.3.en: Zobah: near Damascus, to the northeast of it; some think that it was formerly called “Hobah” (Gen 14:15). It was the capital of the kingdom that ruled over the region of Syria.

18.7.0.en: David wanted to establish his kingdom and extend it toward the Euphrates according to the divine promise (Gen 15:18; Num 24:17)[5].

18.8.0.en: And David took from him a thousand chariots, and seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: David also houghed all the chariot horses, but reserved of them an hundred chariots. [4]

18.8.1.en: It is stated in the Book of Deuteronomy (Deut 17:16) concerning the king, “he shall not multiply horses to himself,” lest he fall into pride, or enter into competition with the kings around him in the signs of pomp and grandeur. Therefore it seems that David kept the hundred chariots as a sign of his victory over Hadarezer and then afterwards destroyed them like the rest of the chariot horses. Some also criticize David, saying that just as he erred in polygamy (1 Chr 14:3), so here he errs in the multiplying of horses.

18.9.0.en: And when the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadarezer king of Zobah, David slew of the Syrians two and twenty thousand men. [5]

18.10.0.en: Then David put garrisons in Syriadamascus; and the Syrians became David’s servants, and brought gifts.

18.10.1.en: Thus the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went. [6]

18.11.0.en: And David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadarezer, and brought them to Jerusalem. [7]

18.11.1.en: David consecrated all the gold, silver and brass materials to the Lord; his son Solomon used them afterwards in building the temple.

18.12.0.en: Likewise from Tibhath, and from Chun, cities of Hadarezer, brought David very much brass, wherewith Solomon made the brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass. [8]

18.12.1.en: Tibhath and Chun: the location of these two cities is not known, nor the relationship between them. In the ancient Arabic text their names are given as Amesa (now Homs) and Baalbek.

18.12.2.en: The writer took care to stress that David took very much brass, and that Solomon made of it the brasen sea, the pillars and the vessels of brass[6].

18.13.0.en: Now when Tou king of Hamath heard how David had smitten all the host of Hadarezer king of Zobah; [9]

18.13.1.en: The kingdom of Tou was on the border of the kingdom of Hadarezer (see 2 Sam 8:8-9).

18.14.0.en: He sent Hadoram his son to king David, to enquire of his welfare, and to congratulate him, because he had fought against Hadarezer, and smitten him; (for Hadarezer had war with Tou).

18.14.1.en: and with him all manner of vessels of gold and silver and brass. [10] 1. It is to our advantage that our friends be among those who enjoy the divine presence. When the king of Hamath heard of the greatness of David’s success, he sent to congratulate him and to win his favor with a valuable gift [9-10].

18.15.0.en: It is not profitable for anyone to oppose the Son of David; therefore “Kiss the Son, lest he be angry” (Ps 2:12). Let the kings and judges of the earth, as well as the lowly, learn and seek wisdom. The gifts we should bring to God are not vessels of gold and silver, for these befit one who has nothing to be brought to him, but we offer Him our hearts and our pure love, as well as ourselves as a living sacrifice. 2. Of the blessing that God bestows abundantly on us we must honor Him; for the gifts of his friends, like the spoils of his enemies, [David dedicated unto God] [11], that is, he kept them for building and adorning the temple, and we ought to dedicate to God, and use for the glory of His name, everything that is true and precious to us: [let our merchandise and our hire be holiness to the LORD] (Isa 23:18). 3. Those who take God with them wherever they go may expect to prosper and be preserved wherever they turn; it was said before [6] and is repeated here also [13], “Thus the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went”; God always helps those whose eyes are always turned toward Him. 4. God gives strength to men not that they may appear great with it, but that they may do good with it; when David reigned over all Israel, he executed judgment and justice among his people, and thus he responded to the result of his exaltation; he was not so focused on his victories abroad that he forgot to do justice at home, and in this he served the divine King, and God [who sitteth on the throne judging right](*), and so he was a prominent type of the Messiah, [whose sceptre of righteousness is the sceptre of his kingdom](**).

18.16.s.en: 4. The defeat of the Edomites and the dedication of the spoils to the Lord

18.16.0.en: 11 Them also king David dedicated unto the LORD, with the silver and the gold that he brought from all these nations; from Edom, and from Moab, and from the children of Ammon, and from the Philistines, and from Amalek. 12 Moreover Abishai the son of Zeruiah slew of the Edomites in the valley of salt eighteen thousand.

18.16.1.en: Them also king David dedicated unto the LORD, with the silver and the gold that he brought from all these nations;

18.16.2.en: from Edom, and from Moab, and from the children of Ammon, and from the Philistines, and from Amalek. [11]

18.16.3.en: The nations used to pay tribute to Israel because of its superiority over the nations and the strength of its authority.

18.16.4.en: David set apart for God the gifts that Tou king of Hamath sent to him, and also the gold and silver he seized as spoils from the nations, since He is the source of everything, and everything must be used for His sake.

18.16.5.en: Thus it is fitting for the believer to consecrate his heart, his gifts and his resources to God and to His glory.

18.17.0.en: Moreover Abishai the son of Zeruiah slew of the Edomites in the valley of salt eighteen thousand. [12]

18.17.1.en: David turned toward the south and overcame the Edomites, and occupied the Gulf of Aqaba, which opens onto the Red Sea and what lies beyond it. Solomon used it afterwards in conducting commercial relations.

18.17.2.en: The eighteen thousand whom Abishai slew were ascribed to David (2 Sam 8:13).

18.18.0.en: And he put garrisons in Edom; and all the Edomites became David’s servants.

18.18.1.en: Thus the LORD preserved David whithersoever he went. [13]

18.18.2.en: The Lord gave David victory wherever he turned. David felt that God was the source of his successive victories, and did not ascribe them to his own skill, experience and personal abilities.

18.19.0.en: So David reigned over all Israel, and executed judgment and justice among all his people. [14]

18.19.1.en: As for his care for justice, King David was the head of justice. The administering of justice was the king’s responsibility (1 Kgs 3:16-28; Isa 11:4; Ps 72).

18.19.2.en: His mission as a king was to “execute judgment and justice among all his people.”

18.19.3.en: His enemies felt David’s wrath, but his people enjoyed his righteousness, his godliness and his justice. David was not only a brave and righteous leader, but also a wise administrator and organizer.

18.20.s.en: 7. Appointments in the army and in government affairs

18.20.0.en: And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the host; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, recorder. [15]

18.20.1.en: The list of those who worked with him given here corresponds to what is stated in (2 Sam 8:16-18).

18.20.2.en: The second man directly after the king was Joab, the commander of the army, who entered into battles for the sake of the kingdom. Besides his command of the army he was the head of the king’s personal guard. The guarding of the king was of the utmost importance, as the cost of the fame he had gained.

18.20.3.en: Some scholars see that King David appointed a recorder after the Egyptian system, who records the events of the state.

18.20.4.en: “The recorder”: David most likely took this system from Egypt; he is like an official spokesman of the royal court, as appears in many Egyptian records, and he is nowadays close to the head of protocol.

18.21.s.en: 8. Appointments in the service of the temple

18.21.0.en: 16 And Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Abimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests; and Shavsha was scribe; 17 And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David were chief about the king.

18.21.1.en: And Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Abimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests; and Shavsha was scribe; [16]

18.21.2.en: Shavsha (Shousha) was the royal secretary, the king’s private secretary and the general secretary of state, and represents what is now the secretary of state. He was responsible for all correspondence and for the revenues of the temple, and had an important role in the general affairs of the state.

18.21.3.en: The mention of the two priests with these high leading figures in the affairs of the state reveals the strong link between the affairs of the state and the religious life of the people.

18.22.0.en: And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David were chief about the king. [17]

18.22.1.en: It is most likely that the Cherethites and the Pelethites were a company of foreign soldiers who joined David during his flight from Saul, and remained loyal to him throughout his reign (2 Sam 15:17-18), and became part of his personal guard.

18.22.2.en: This list of military, civil and religious leaders mentions the first sons of David; in (2 Sam 8:18) it mentions them as priests, but here it mentions them as chiefs and leaders in the king’s service, since the priests had become Levites.

18.22.3.en: It is stated in (2 Sam 8:18) that “David’s sons were priests,” not for performing priestly work such as offering sacrifices, but for their carrying out some administrative work of the temple. The First Book of Chronicles made this clear, for it said that David’s sons were chief officers in the king’s service.

18.22.4.en: From Your hand come victory and success

18.22.5.en: v Despite the courage that marked David from his youth, he realized that the secret of his courage was his clinging to You.

18.22.6.en: In all his battles he does not move without You.

18.22.7.en: He hides in You, and so enjoys victory.

18.22.8.en: Grant me, in my constant battle with the devil, not to rely on past victories.

18.22.9.en: You are the secret of holiness, purity and victory.

18.22.10.en: Your grace is my support, and Your presence in my depths is the secret of my continual building up.

18.22.11.en: v Grant me, together with trust in You, to be careful to grow constantly in You.

18.22.12.en: David’s victories over the surrounding nations did not distract him from caring for his whole people and judging them with justice.

18.22.13.en: Grant me that my victory over some sins may not distract me from caring to surrender all my life to You.

18.22.14.en: Let me take shelter in Your righteousness and hold fast to Your commandments.

18.22.15.en: v His victories did not distract him from sound administration, in his army and in the affairs of the state.

18.22.16.en: Let me cling to You and enjoy wisdom and good counsel.

18.22.17.en: Then all that is within me will be under an administration worthy of Your children.

18.22.18.en: Glory to You, O Giver of victory, wisdom and counsel.

18.22.19.en: Glory to You, who care for all that is within me and all that is outside me.

18.22.20.en: You are the true Leader of all my life.
